title: Trump University Forced to Drop “University” Name for Lack of License
description_short: Trump University Forced to Drop “University” Name for Lack of License
description_medium: New York State education officials told Trump that his business could not call itself a “university” because it lacked a license and did not meet legal definitions. The program was renamed the Trump Entrepreneur Institute in 2011. The episode underscored regulatory concerns about how the business was marketed to consumers.
description_long: Trump's real estate education business changed its name to the Trump Entrepreneur Institute in 2011 after New York education officials objected to its use of the word university. Officials said the enterprise lacked a license and did not meet the legal definition of a university. The name change concerned a commercial seminar program that used Trump's celebrity and promised instruction in real estate investing. Customers paid between $1,495 and $35,000 for courses and mentorship offerings. Complaints about the program continued after the rebranding. In 2013, Attorney General Eric Schneiderman filed a civil lawsuit alleging deceptive marketing, inadequate instruction and failures to deliver promised mentoring. Trump and his lawyer denied fraud and called the lawsuit politically motivated. The regulatory naming dispute therefore preceded a separate consumer-protection case. Renaming the business complied with the demand to stop using the university label, but did not resolve the later allegations about what students had been promised or received.

title: Trump Removes NLRB Member and Two EEOC Commissioners, Leaving Both Bodies Without Quorums
description_short: Trump Removes NLRB Member and Two EEOC Commissioners, Leaving Both Bodies Without Quorums
description_medium: On January 27, 2025, President Trump removed NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and fired two Democratic EEOC commissioners, Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels. The removals left both independent bodies without the quorum required for some commission- or board-level decisions. The NLRB's regional enforcement work continued, but the Board could not issue decisions without a quorum.
description_long: On January 27, 2025, Trump removed Gwynne Wilcox from the National Labor Relations Board and dismissed two Democratic Equal Employment Opportunity Commission members, Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels. He also removed NLRB General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo. The membership changes left both bodies below the quorum needed for certain collective decisions. Other members remained in office, and the NLRB's regional enforcement work continued even though its Board could not issue decisions. Wilcox's dismissal came well before the expiration of her Senate-confirmed term in August 2028. She had begun her second term in September 2023 and served as Board chair from December 17, 2024, until January 20, 2025. She was the first Black woman to serve on the NLRB and to chair it. The dismissals combined an interruption in board-level decision-making with the removal of officials serving established terms; the agencies' remaining operations continued within those institutional limits.

title: Trump: ‘Grind the country to a halt’: Democrat urges national strike if Trump meddles in midterms
description_short: Trump: ‘Grind the country to a halt’: Democrat urges national strike if Trump meddles in midterms
description_medium: ‘Grind the country to a halt’: Democrat urges national strike if Trump meddles in midterms. In wake of Donald Trump’s call for Republicans to ‘take over’ voting, senator Ruben Gallego urges citizens to take a stand and give the ‘ultimate response’ This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego proposed a national strike if Trump interfered with the November 2026 midterm elections. Speaking on the Court of History podcast, he urged workers, including pilots, train drivers and teachers, to withhold their labor if officials seized ballot boxes, stopped counting or surrounded polling places. His proposal followed Trump's call for Republicans to take control of voting in at least 15 unspecified locations, accompanied by false claims of widespread election fraud. Gallego argued that democratic stability was necessary for economic stability and warned that interference could provoke an economic shutdown. The dispute also included former Trump adviser Steve Bannon's suggestion that ICE agents surround polling sites. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said she had not heard Trump discuss formal plans to place ICE outside polling locations, while declining to guarantee agents would not be nearby. Gallego's call was conditional: he advocated a response to possible election interference rather than announcing an ongoing strike.
